rv.q: Even at its most extreme, The Steel Man is all too real, and its current staging makes for an unforgettable night at the theatre.
The Steel Man is a forceful, humane, and deeply affecting theatrical experience, one that lingers well beyond the final scene.
Yet much of the time we are moved by these less than perfect individuals who struggle to understand, accept, and move on.
The potential for volcanic-level eruptions and suspense throughout are riveting, and a surprise ending brings some level of closure.
It is a worthwhile production, and it reminds us of the long shadow cast by unnecessary wars, waged at enormous human cost for the enrichment of a privileged few.
The story is realistic and sympathetic, yet dramatization just misses.
What it lacks is the emotional complexity that would allow its central relationship to transcend cruelty and obligation.

cn.t: Critics praise *The Steel Man* as a forceful, deeply affecting drama of intergenerational trauma, bolstered by superb performances. Gitter's work earns strong acclaim for its emotional power and unflinching portrayal of a Holocaust survivor's lasting impact on his family.
